answer:
DPO optimizes a relative chosen/rejected log-ratio, so both absolute probabilities can decrease while the preferred response decreases less. Noisy or separable preference data can also encourage excessive margins; length and reference-policy effects complicate evaluation. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)

IPO uses a squared target for a preference-related log-ratio rather than continually increasing a logistic margin. KTO learns from individual desirable/undesirable labels using a prospect-theoretic utility formulation. SimPO uses length-normalized sequence log probability and a target margin without a separate reference model. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12036) [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306) [4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734)

These are different objectives, not universal fixes for every DPO failure. Compare absolute likelihoods, length distributions, win rates under controlled judging, and out-of-distribution tasks. Preserve the distinction between an observed training dynamic and proof that a new objective improves the underlying human preference.
